task.name: Preflight scoring distinguishes a story beyond reasonable single-story scope from the largest coherent one
task.story_text:
## What

Preflight scoring distinguishes a story that exceeds reasonable single-story scope from the
largest story that is still coherent as one unit. Score 9 means the largest reasonable coherent
story; score 10 means the work is beyond what one story should attempt and should be decomposed.

Routing does not change. This is a scoring-semantics contract, not a routing-granularity change.

## Why

Score 10 has never been assigned. Over 448 scored runs in the audit substrate it appears zero
times, while 8 alone is 22.3% and 8+9 together are 29.5%.

The cause is in the scoring guidance, not in code: the anchor table merges 9 and 10 into one
description written at epic/subsystem scope — new subsystem, rewrite of a state-machine phase,
coordinated cross-codebase migration. The epic and sub-issue convention splits work of that
scope into slices before a story is ever scored, so nothing preflight sees can reach the
bucket's extreme end, and nothing in the text says where a 9 ends and a 10 begins.

The operator cost is that the top of the scale stops discriminating. A 9 reads the same whether
the story is ordinarily large or four stories in a trenchcoat. The diagnosis-portability epic
scored 9, ran twice for $43.64, never reached DEV, and split by hand into four pieces scoring
7, 8, 8 and 6 that landed for $86.11 — a judgment the operator made after the money was spent,
from evidence preflight already held.

**This does not reopen #1019.** That decision settled how coarsely the score is *consumed* —
model tiers, reviewer counts and reasoning effort route through deliberately coarse buckets,
and `routing-policy.md` records that as intended rather than a defect. It did not assign a
meaning to 10 as distinct from 9. Consumption granularity and scoring semantics are independent:
9 and 10 can continue to select identical models and reviewers while meaning different things
about whether the work is one story.

## Acceptance criteria

- The scoring guidance gives 9 and 10 mutually exclusive rubrics: 10 states that the work
  exceeds what a single story should attempt, and 9 states the largest scope still coherent as
  one story. Neither rubric admits a case the other also admits.
- No routing bucket moves. Scores 9 and 10 continue to resolve to the same model tier, reviewer
  count and reasoning effort on every axis, and the routing tests pass unchanged.
- The scope-exceeded meaning is carried by the implementation-complexity axis rather than by a
  combined or projected score, so a story that is validation-heavy but cohesive as one unit is
  not reported as exceeding scope.
- A story assessed as exceeding scope reports that as a distinct signal a consumer can read
  directly, rather than requiring the consumer to infer it from the numeric value.
- Stories that score below the ceiling are unaffected: recorded scores keep the routing outcome
  they resolve to today, and no story that scores 9 changes tier as a result of this change.

## Example

Today, both readings of "very large" collapse onto 9:

```
story: "port diagnosis across projects"     -> 9   (was four stories: 7,8,8,6)
story: "cross-module refactor, one seam"    -> 9   (genuinely one story)
routing for both                            -> strong dev, max reviewers
```

After:

```
story: "port diagnosis across projects"     -> 10  scope_exceeded
story: "cross-module refactor, one seam"    ->  9
routing for both                            -> strong dev, max reviewers   (unchanged)
```

The routing row is identical on purpose. What changes is that the first story is now
distinguishable as one that should not be attempted whole.

handoff.summary: Split the preflight scoring ceiling into mutually exclusive 9 and 10 rubrics and threaded a new scope_exceeded boolean through preflight state, artifact, forge.log phase_end, audit block, resume record, routing record, and the preflight cache. The signal is derived from the implementation-complexity axis reaching 10 (COMPLEXITY_SCORE_MAX) after dual-axis projection, so a validation-heavy but cohesive story whose projected complexity_score is lifted is never reported as exceeding scope. A classifier-emitted scope_exceeded that contradicts its own implementation score is recorded as a preflight warning rather than obeyed — the numeric axis stays authoritative; this is asserted as a recorded decision in the seam tests. No routing implementation or bucket table was touched; a new regression test asserts 9 and 10 resolve identically on dev tier, plan tier, reviewer count, and per-phase reasoning effort. routing-policy.md documents that 9 and 10 route identically by design and that scope_exceeded is the readable signal.

plan_review.findings:
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 1 has the model emit scope_exceeded, but Step 2 discards it in favor of deriving from implementation score == 10. Every coordinator score-mutating path caps below 10 (override floor 8, ambiguity floor 5, agent-failure hard-set 9), so a model that emits scope_exceeded: true while its implementation score is 9 or lower will always have the signal dropped to false. The plan says only 'warning if it disagrees'.
  Suggestion: Decide explicitly whether a model-emitted true with a sub-10 implementation score is a warning-only disagreement (current plan) or should raise the implementation score; if warning-only, assert that behavior in the Step 4 parser tests so it is a recorded decision rather than an accident.
- [P2] [anthropic-opus-cli] docs/guides/routing-policy.md appeared in preflight likely_files but no plan step updates it. It documents what the complexity score controls and currently describes the coarse buckets without any 9-vs-10 semantic distinction, so it will be stale on the new scope_exceeded signal.
  Suggestion: Add a short note to routing-policy.md stating that 9 and 10 route identically by design while meaning different things about single-story coherence, and that scope_exceeded is the readable signal.
